baseband|baseband transmission: Sending a digital signal over a channel **without changing** it to an analog signal. Requires a low-pass channel and a dedicated medium; the required bandwidth is proportional to the bit rate. Example: a wired LAN. See [Baseband & broadband](#/comp3721-w3/baseband-broadband).
broadband|broadband transmission|modulat: Changing the digital signal to an analog signal for transmission. Requires a bandpass channel and a converter (modem) at each end. Examples: a telephone subscriber line, digital cellular phones. See [Baseband & broadband](#/comp3721-w3/baseband-broadband).
low-pass|low-pass channel: A channel that primarily passes signals below a certain frequency: the lowest frequency contained in the channel is zero and it has an upper bound. Less common in real life. See [Baseband & broadband](#/comp3721-w3/baseband-broadband).
bandpass|bandpass channel: A channel that allows signals to pass between two frequency limits, so its bandwidth does not start from zero. More available than a low-pass channel; a digital signal must be converted to analog before it is sent on one. See [Baseband & broadband](#/comp3721-w3/baseband-broadband).
modem: Modulator/demodulator: the converter that changes a digital signal to analog at the sender (digital/analog converter) and back to digital at the receiving end (analog/digital converter). See [Baseband & broadband](#/comp3721-w3/baseband-broadband).
attenuation: Loss of energy to overcome the resistance of the medium. An amplifier compensates for the loss. In decibels an attenuated signal has a negative value. See [Attenuation & the decibel](#/comp3721-w3/attenuation-decibel).
dB|decibel: Measures the relative strengths of two signals or one signal at two different points: $\text{dB} = 10 \log_{10}(P_2/P_1) = 20 \log_{10}(V_2/V_1)$. Negative if attenuated, positive if amplified; half the power is $-3$ dB. See [Attenuation & the decibel](#/comp3721-w3/attenuation-decibel).
dB/km: The usual way to define the loss in a cable. Multiply by the length in km for the decibels of the whole cable: 5 km at $-0.3$ dB/km is $-1.5$ dB. See [E03, worked](#/comp3721-w3/e03-worked).
distortion: The signal changes its form or shape. Can occur in a composite signal made of different frequencies: the components at the receiver have phases different from what they had at the sender. See [Distortion, noise & SNR](#/comp3721-w3/distortion-noise-snr).
noise: Thermal (random motion of electrons in a wire), induced (motors and appliances), crosstalk (the effect of one wire on the other) and impulse (a spike from power lines, lightning). See [Distortion, noise & SNR](#/comp3721-w3/distortion-noise-snr).
SNR|signal-to-noise ratio: Average signal power divided by average noise power: what is wanted over what is not wanted. High SNR means the signal is less corrupted by noise. A ratio of two powers, so it has no unit. See [Distortion, noise & SNR](#/comp3721-w3/distortion-noise-snr).
SNRdB: SNR in decibel units: $\text{SNR}_{dB} = 10 \log_{10} \text{SNR}$, so an SNR of 10000 is 40 dB. Turn it back into a ratio with $10^{\text{SNR}_{dB}/10}$ before using the Shannon formula. See [Distortion, noise & SNR](#/comp3721-w3/distortion-noise-snr).
BitRate|Nyquist|Nyquist bit rate: Theoretical maximum bit rate of a **noiseless** channel: $\text{BitRate} = 2 \times \text{bandwidth} \times \log_{2} L$. See [Nyquist bit rate](#/comp3721-w3/nyquist).
L|levels|signal levels: The number of signal levels in the Nyquist formula. Increasing the levels may reduce the reliability of the system; a result that is not a power of 2 means increasing the levels or reducing the bit rate. See [Nyquist bit rate](#/comp3721-w3/nyquist).
C|Capacity|capacity|Shannon|Shannon capa: Theoretical highest data rate of a **noisy** channel: $\text{Capacity} = \text{bandwidth} \times \log_{2}(1 + \text{SNR})$. No number of signal levels achieves a data rate above it. See [Shannon capacity](#/comp3721-w3/shannon).
B|bandwidth: Two contexts. In **hertz**: the range of frequencies in a composite signal, or that a channel can pass. In **bits per second**: the number of bits per second a channel, a link or a network can transmit, which we call bit rate. See [Bandwidth](#/comp3721-w3/bandwidth-delay).
bandwidth-delay product: The number of bits that can fill the link: bandwidth (in bps) × delay. To use the maximum capability of a full-duplex link the burst size is 2 × bandwidth × delay. See [Bandwidth](#/comp3721-w3/bandwidth-delay).
parallel|parallel transmission: The $n$ bits of a group are sent together on $n$ lines. Advantage: speed (a factor of $n$ over serial). Disadvantage: cost. See [Transmission modes](#/comp3721-w3/transmission-modes).
serial|serial transmission: The bits are sent one after another on one line, which reduces the cost over parallel by roughly a factor of $n$. Needs a parallel/serial converter at the sender and a serial/parallel converter at the receiver. See [Transmission modes](#/comp3721-w3/transmission-modes).
USB: Universal Serial Bus. USB 1.0 12 Mbps, USB 2.0 480 Mbps, USB 3.2 Gen 1 5 Gbps, Gen 2 10 Gbps, Gen 2x2 20 Gbps. See [Transmission modes](#/comp3721-w3/transmission-modes).
